I like how mornings feel when the world is still negotiating with itself. Streetlights give up gradually, puddles hold onto last night’s sky, and even the boldest sounds seem to arrive cautiously—as if they’re checking whether you’re awake enough to receive them. There’s a particular kind of quiet that isn’t emptiness at all. It’s fullness, just not the kind you can name. It’s the hum of possibility in the walls, the soft insistence of time moving forward, the first inhale of a day that hasn’t decided what it wants from you yet.

Sometimes I think imagination is a form of weather. It changes pressure in the mind; it shifts the air. You can walk through the same street and feel utterly different versions of it—one day ordinary and practical, the next day lit from within like a stage set. A coffee shop becomes a harbor. A bus stop becomes a checkpoint between lives. Even the smallest ordinary objects—keys, receipts, a cracked phone screen—take on narrative weight, as though they’re props handed to you for a story you haven’t started reading.

By afternoon, the day insists on facts. By evening, it returns to mood. And at night, when everything finally slows, I find myself grateful for the contradictions: how we can be both tired and curious, both finished and unfinished. Tomorrow will come anyway. The question is simply what we’ll do with the first moment we notice it arriving.
